summary: This experimental memo extends L2TP, a tunnelling method for PPP, so that tunnels can carry multicast traffic efficiently. It is aimed at deployments where multicast services have to be delivered through L2TP tunnels.

eli5.summary: Sending the same video to many people through many separate pipes wastes effort. This experimental idea lets one tunnel carry shared traffic more efficiently.

questions: how does multicast work over l2tp
why send multicast only once through an l2tp tunnel
what is an outgoing sessions list
how does the lns track multicast subscriptions
subtitle: Efficient forwarding of multicast streams through L2TP tunnels

tldr.problem: L2TP tunnels normally carry unicast traffic and do not support multicast. Video or IPTV services delivered through L2TP require sending the same multicast stream multiple times, once per tunnel—wasting bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: Extensions allow a single L2TP multicast session to carry one multicast flow through a tunnel, with the tunnel concentrator replicating it to each end-user. The LNS sends the multicast traffic once; the LAC does the replication.
tldr.outcome: Multicast services can run efficiently through L2TP tunnels, sparing the core network from redundant copies and allowing operators to deploy IPTV and similar services to users who connect via L2TP.

facts.label: Default session threshold
facts.value: 2 users (creates session when 2 or more users request same group)

facts.label: New AVPs
facts.value: 5 (Multicast Capability, New Outgoing Sessions, Acknowledgement, Withdraw, Priority)

today: RFC 4045 is Experimental and remains unobsoleted. It defines an optional extension for IPTV and multicast service delivery through L2TP, adopted by some operators but not universally deployed.

sections.title: The Multicast Problem in L2TP
sections.content:
L2TP is commonly used to connect broadband users (via xDSL and cable) to a central network through unicast sessions. When multicast services like IPTV need to reach users over L2TP tunnels, the LNS (the central server) must replicate each multicast flow once for every unicast session that requested it. If 100 users in the same tunnel want to watch the same channel, the LNS sends the stream 100 times through the tunnel, once per session.

This document defines an extension that allows a single L2TP multicast session to carry each multicast flow. The LAC (tunnel concentrator on the access side) receives the stream once and replicates it to the appropriate users locally. This reduces the load on the network between the LAC and LNS and allows the LNS to scale to more users.
sections.eli5: Without the extension: the LNS sends the same TV channel 100 times through the tunnel to 100 users—100 copies of the same video use up the tunnel's capacity. With the extension: the LNS sends it once, the LAC copies it, and saves 99 copies of bandwidth.

sections.title: How Multicast Sessions Work
sections.content:
Multicast delivery through L2TP requires three steps. First, the LAC advertises its multicast capability to the LNS when setting up the L2TP control connection, using a new Multicast Capability AVP. Second, the LNS tracks which users want which multicast groups (using IGMP or MLD messages from users). Third, when a group has enough subscribers (a configurable threshold, default of 2), the LNS opens a dedicated L2TP multicast session for that group and sends the stream into it.

The LAC maintains an Outgoing Session List (OSL) for each multicast session, identifying which unicast sessions should receive the multicast traffic. The LNS updates this list as users join and leave multicast groups. The LNS can also assign a priority level for multicast traffic relative to unicast traffic on each session or globally.
sections.eli5: The LNS watches which users want to watch which channel. When enough people want the same channel, it opens a dedicated virtual pipe (multicast session) for that channel and tells the LAC: send this to users 5, 12, and 18.

sections.title: Opening and Managing Multicast Sessions
sections.content:
The LNS initiates multicast session setup using a three-message exchange: MSRQ (Multicast-Session-Request), MSRP (response), and MSE (Multicast-Session-Establishment). Once established, the LNS sends Multicast-Session-Information (MSI) control messages to keep the LAC's OSL in sync. MSI messages carry new outgoing sessions (added by the LNS), acknowledge which sessions are ready to receive traffic, and withdraw sessions when users leave.

The LNS may also include a Maximum BPS value in the MSRQ, telling the LAC how fast the multicast traffic can flow. This protects against a single high-bandwidth stream flooding users with low-speed links. Sessions are torn down passively (by emptying the OSL) or actively (with a Multicast-Session-End-Notify message) when no users remain.
sections.eli5: The LNS calls the LAC and says: set up a multicast session. The LAC gets ready. The LNS says: send this channel to users A, B, and C. Later: user A left, remove them from the list. Finally: nobody wants this channel anymore, shut it down.

sections.title: Tracking Group Membership States
sections.content:
The LNS acts as a multicast router, running IGMP (for IPv4) or MLD (for IPv6) to learn which users want which groups. For each L2TP tunnel, the LNS computes a merged group state by combining the membership reports from all unicast sessions in the tunnel. If user 1 wants group 224.0.0.1 from source S1 and user 2 wants it from S2, the merged state is S1 and S2.

The LNS can employ different replication strategies. For INCLUDE mode (when users specify sources they want), it can create one multicast session per source-group pair or one per group. For EXCLUDE mode (when users exclude certain sources), it creates one session per excluded-source-list—sending all sources except those explicitly excluded. This design ensures that users sharing a tunnel get the same multicast behavior they would on a shared ethernet network.
sections.eli5: If User A wants football from channel 1 and User B wants football from channel 2, the LNS sends both channel 1 and 2 to both users—same as if they shared one WiFi network. If User C says no sports, the LNS still sends sports to A and B but not to C.

sections.title: Compatibility and Traffic Merging
sections.content:
The extension does not affect standard L2TP unicast operation. LACs and LNSs that do not support multicast simply ignore the new AVPs and messages. A mixed network of supporting and non-supporting equipment can coexist.

Because multicast packets leaving the LNS are pure IP packets (not PPP-framed), while unicast traffic is PPP-framed, the LAC must merge the two streams correctly for each user. The LAC frames multicast packets according to each user's PPP parameters before sending them. This differs from standard multicast routing, where a LAC forwards IP packets as-is, but it ensures each user receives properly framed data regardless of whether the traffic came from a unicast or multicast session.
sections.eli5: Old LACs and LNSs ignore the new extension—they just do unicast as before. New ones support both. When putting packets on the wire to a user, the LAC wraps them the same way whether they came from unicast or multicast, so the user does not need to know the difference.
